newsitem.title: USA: PacifiCorp to acquire Britain's Energy Group. [corrected 19:24 gmt]
newsitem.headline: PacifiCorp to acquire Britain's Energy Group. [corrected 19:24 gmt]

text.p: PacifiCorp said on Friday it has agreed to acquire Britain's Energy Group Plc for $9.6 billion in a deal that would create one of the world's most powerful energy companies.

As part of the deal, PacifiCorp will sell its Pacific Telecom unit to Century Telephone Enterprises Inc. for $1.5 billion in cash. (Corrects by deleting reference to debt to make clear that PacifiCorp is not retaining Pacific Telecom's debt.)
The deal is the latest takeover of a British electric utility by U.S. companies eager to grab a share in the country's market, which will be deregulated in 1998.

The merged company will have 5 million electric and gas customers, 17,000 megawatts of generation capacity and more than 10 billion tons of coal reserves. It will employ 26,000 workers in Britain, the United States and Australia.
The companies said they did not expect the merger to result in significant job cuts.

PacifiCorp, which operates in seven U.S. states and Australia, said it will pay 6.955 pounds sterling ($11.35) a share for Energy Group. It will also assume $3.8 billion of debt held by Britain's biggest electricity distributor.

"Our strategic focus is to become a leading global energy provider," President Fred Buckman said in a statement. "This transaction focuses PacifiCorp squarely on the energy sector and will enable us to better meet the diversified energy needs of our customers."
PacifiCorp, based in Portland, Ore., said it also plans to sell other non-core assets, including PacifiCorp Financial Services and Pacific Generation Co.
PacifiCorp will make the acquisition through PacifiCorp Holdings Inc., which will finance the cash deal through borrowings and the sale of its non-core assets, it said.
The merger is expected to boost PacifiCorp's earnings as of the first year after it closes, the company said.
The deal has been approved by the boards of directors of both companies, and remains subject to regulatory approval in Britain and antitrust clearance in the United States.

Energy Group, which includes Britain's biggest electricity supplier, Eastern Electricity, and U.S.-Australian coal producer Peabody, has been considered a takeover target since it was spun off from once-mighty industrial conglomerate Hanson Plc in February.
The company was forced to announce that it was in talks over a possible merger agreement on Tuesday after its share price rose strongly on the London stock exchange.

But regulatory concerns kept Energy Group's shares trading below the bid price, even though the company had reported a 30 percent surge in operating income to 317 million pounds for the six months ended March 31, analysts said.
Energy Group shares were up 3 pence (4.9 cents) at 650 pence ($10.60) in early afternoon trading on the LSE.
"There's much more uncertainty over this deal, with a new and untried Labour government and the possibility of a windfall tax," said one London analyst who asked not to be identified.

The new Labour government, which swept to power in a landslide victory May 1, was fiercely critical of the previous government's takeover policy under which all but one of Britain's original 12 regional electricity companies (Recs) were swallowed up by buyers.
Privatised utilities also face a one-time tax on excess profits, which the government has vowed to include in its first budget on July 2.
Uncertainty over which companies would be hit by the tax and by how much has kept utility shares under pressure in recent months, with many trading at discounts to the market.
But analysts said there was scant reason on competitive or regulatory grounds for the new Labour government to block a takeover.
"I can't see any obvious problems for the government. The Rec has already been taken over so largely it's just a change of ownership rather than structure," the analyst said.
Some analysts believe the new government might call for customer compensation in the form of price cuts to approve the bid.
PacifiCorp's stock was unchanged at $22.25, while Century rose 87.5 cents to $32.625 on the New York Stock Exchange at mid-morning.
